[[Heathrow Express]] | website = {{Official URL}} | footnotes = }} '''Heathrow Airport Holdings''' is a company that operates and manages [[Heathrow Airport]] based in [[London]], England. It was formed by the privatisation of the '''British Airports Authority''' as '''BAA plc'''{{Cite web|url=https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/01970855|title=LHR AIRPORTS LIMITED - Overview (free company information from Companies House)|website=find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk|access-date=18 April 2021|archive-date=18 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210418195159/https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/01970855|url-status=live}} as part of [[Margaret Thatcher]]'s privatisation of government-owned assets, and was once a constituent of the [[FTSE 100 Index]]. BAA plc was bought in 2006 by a consortium led by [[Ferrovial]], a [[Spain|Spanish]] firm specialising in the construction and operation of transport and urban infrastructure. In March 2009, the company was eventually required to sell [[Gatwick Airport|Gatwick]] and [[London Stansted Airport|Stansted]] airports; eventually BAA sold all its airports other than Heathrow and was renamed to its current name in 2012 to reflect its main business; businesses sold include the management of airports in the [[United States|US]] and [[Africa]], as well as the retailer [[World Duty Free]]. In 2024, Ferrovial sold most of its shares to the private capital [[Ardian (company)|Ardian]] and the Saudi [[Public Investment Fund]], now among other foreign institutional investors. The company's head office is in the [[Compass Centre]], on the grounds of Heathrow Airport in the [[London Borough of Hillingdon]]. The company makes money from charging [[landing fee]]s and departing passenger levies to airlines, and from ancillary operations within those airports such as retail, car parking and property. ==History== [[File:LHR London, England (Heathrow Airport), United Kingdom PP1367853288.jpg|thumb|Heathrow Airport accounts for 95% of the company's business]] ===British Airports Authority=== The British Airports Authority was established by the '''{{visible anchor|Airport Authority Act 1965}}''', to take responsibility for four state-owned airports from the Ministry of Aviation – [[Heathrow Airport]], [[Gatwick Airport]], [[Glasgow Prestwick Airport|Prestwick Airport]] and [[Stansted Airport]]. In the following few years, the authority acquired [[Edinburgh Airport]] (1971), [[Glasgow Airport]] (1975) and [[Aberdeen Airport]] (1975). The authority took on the [[Ministry of Civil Aviation Constabulary]] in 1966, which was renamed to become the [[British Airports Authority Constabulary]], and was disbanded between 1974 and 1975. As part of [[Margaret Thatcher]]'s moves to privatise government owned assets, the [[Airports Act 1986]] was passed which mandated the creation of BAA plc as a vehicle by which stock market funds could be raised. The initial capitalisation of BAA plc was £1,225 million. In the early 1990s, the company sold Prestwick International Airport (now known as [[Glasgow Prestwick Airport]]). ===International operations and takeover=== BAA won a contract to manage the retail operations at [[Pittsburgh International Airport]] in 1991 through its [[BAA USA]] subsidiary.Wulf Teiwes and Morten Tveit, London Business School, http://faculty.london.edu/cvoss/baa/html/baagoes.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190923044043/http://faculty.london.edu/cvoss/baa/html/baagoes.htm |date=23 September 2019 }} In 1995, BAA was became a [[Cross listing|cross listed company]] when listed on the [[Australian Securities Exchange]] in anticipation of the privatisation of the [[Federal Airports Corporation]]'s airports.BAA listed on Stock Exchange ''[[Australian Aviation]]'' issue 106 May 1995 page 6 It was delisted in July 1998.[https://www.asx.com.au/asx/v2/statistics/displayAnnouncement.do?display=text&issuerId=3198&announcementId=592403&documentDate=1998-07-03&documentNumber=163061 Suspension from Official Quotation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251227131855/https://www.asx.com.au/asx/v2/statistics/displayAnnouncement.do?announcementId=592403&documentDate=1998-07-03&documentNumber=163061&display=text&issuerId=3198 |date=27 December 2025 }} [[Australian Securities Exchange]] 3 July 1998 In December 2005, BAA made a winning bid of £1.2 billion for a 75% stake in [[Budapest Ferihegy International Airport]], the largest airport in [[Hungary]], which was being privatised by the Hungarian government. In July 2006, BAA was taken over by a consortium led by [[Ferrovial]], following a bid which valued the company at £10.1 billion ($20 billion).''The Economist'', [http://www.economist.com/people/displaystory.cfm?story_id=9440733 ''The man who bought trouble''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090213192644/http://www.economist.com/people/displaystory.cfm?story_id=9440733 |date=13 February 2009 }}. Consulted on 18 July 2007. As a result, the company was [[delisted]] from the [[London Stock Exchange]] (where it had previously been part of the FTSE 100 Index) on 15 August 2006. Following the take-over, the decision was made to sell the stake in Ferihegy and this was completed in June 2007, when a consortium led by [[Hochtief AirPort]] of Germany purchased the stake.{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/4511168.stm |title=BAA closing in on Hungarian deal |work=[[BBC News]] |date=8 December 2005 |access-date=7 July 2009 |archive-date=12 December 2005 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051212060441/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/4511168.stm |url-status=live }} BAA expanded into international operations, including retail contracts at [[Logan International Airport]] and [[Baltimore-Washington International Airport]] (through BAA USA), and a management contract with the City of [[Indianapolis]] to run the [[Indianapolis International Airport]] (as BAA Indianapolis, Inc.) before ultimately selling off its US division to Prospect Capital Corporation in July 2010.[http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/baa-usa-acquired-by-new-owners-to-be-renamed-airmall-usa-99758559.html BAA USA Acquired by New Owners, to be Renamed] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150306061605/http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/baa-usa-acquired-by-new-owners-to-be-renamed-airmall-usa-99758559.html |date=6 March 2015 }} [[PR Newswire]] Retrieved on 16 August 2013. === Divestitures under Ferrovial === After an inquiry which ran from August 2008 to March 2009,{{cite news |last1=Osborne |first1=Alastair |last2=Butler |first2=Sarah |date=17 August 2008 |title=Commission to break up BAA monopoly |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/transport/2794915/Commission-to-break-up-BAA-monopoly.html |newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|access-date=20 October 2014}} the UK [[Competition Commission (United Kingdom)|Competition Commission]] announced that BAA would be required to sell three of the seven UK airports it owned at the time within two years, over fears the monopoly position held by BAA over London and [[Scotland]]'s airports could have "adverse effects for both passengers and airlines". These were Gatwick, Stansted and either Glasgow or Edinburgh airports. The sales were forecast to raise between £3.5bn and £4bn.{{Cite news | url = https://www.ft.com/content/3adfd1a8-1463-11de-8cd1-0000779fd2ac | newspaper = Financial Times | last = Done | first = Kevin | title = BAA ordered to sell three airports | date=18 March 2009 | access-date = 18 March 2009 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090422211001/http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/3adfd1a8-1463-11de-8cd1-0000779fd2ac.html| archive-date=22 April 2009| url-status= live}}{{cite news|title=BAA to be forced to sell Gatwick, Stansted and Edinburgh airports|newspaper=The Daily Telegraph|location=London|last=Dunkley|first=Jamie|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/transport/3810403/BAA-forced-to-sell-Gatwick-Stanstead-and-Edinburgh-airports.html|access-date=16 January 2019|archive-date=16 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190116150003/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/transport/3810403/BAA-forced-to-sell-Gatwick-Stanstead-and-Edinburgh-airports.html|url-status=live}} BAA announced plans to sell Gatwick Airport on 17 September 2009. At that time, the airport was valued at £1.8bn by regulators and it appeared that several firms including [[Macquarie Group]], [[Manchester Airports Group]], [[Fraport]] and [[Virgin Atlantic]] were interested in this sale, either on their own or as part of a consortium of companies.{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/7620293.stm|title=Gatwick Airport put up for sale|date=17 September 2008|publisher=BBC|access-date=2 November 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090930101836/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/7620293.stm| archive-date= 30 September 2009 | url-status= live}} Ferrovial and its partners ([[Government of Singapore Investment Corporation]] and the [[Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec]]) had been seeking £1.8bn to £2bn when they opened the bidding process. Eventually, the sale was confirmed on 21 October 2009 and formally completed on 3 December 2009, for a fee of £1.51 billion, almost 25 per cent less than BAA had expected Gatwick would fetch when the sale was announced a year previously. BAA sold the airport to [[Global Infrastructure Partners]], the fund backed by [[Credit Suisse]] and [[General Electric]], who also operate [[London City Airport]]. Ferrovial, the majority holder in BAA, said that it expected to make a capital loss of around 142 million euros (US$212.6 million) against its consolidated earnings following the sale.{{cite news|url=http://uk.reuters.com/article/idUKTRE59K1D820091021|title=BAA sells Gatwick airport at a loss|date=21 October 2009|publisher=Reuters|access-date=2 November 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091023005901/http://uk.reuters.com/article/idUKTRE59K1D820091021| archive-date= 23 October 2009 | url-status= dead}} In October 2011, BAA announced that [[Edinburgh Airport]] would be put up for sale in early 2012 with an aim to handing over the running of the site to a new owner by summer 2012.{{cite news|title=BAA to sell Edinburgh Airport over competition rules|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-edinburgh-east-fife-15367555|website=[[BBC News]]|location=[[Edinburgh]]|publisher=[[BBC Scotland]]|date=19 October 2011|access-date=20 October 2012|archive-date=11 June 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120611030045/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-edinburgh-east-fife-15367555|url-status=live}} Numerous groups were reported to have expressed interest, including a consortium of Scottish businesses headed by former Edinburgh Airport Manager, and Fraport, the owners of [[Frankfurt Airport]], Germany. The airport was sold to [[Global Infrastructure Partners]] in 2012. Later that year, the company name was changed to Heathrow Airport Holdings Limited. In January 2013, it was announced that Stansted would be sold to the Manchester Airports Group, a holding company owned by the 10 borough councils of Greater Manchester. In May 2014, Heathrow Airport Holdings announced the appointment of John Holland-Kaye, current Development Director, as chief executive officer, succeeding Colin Matthews on 1 July 2014.{{cite web |url=http://mediacentre.heathrowairport.com/Press-releases/Heathrow-announces-new-Chief-Executive-Officer-8c2.aspx |title=Heathrow - Press releases - Heathrow announces new Chief Executive Officer |access-date=15 May 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140516045654/http://mediacentre.heathrowairport.com/Press-releases/Heathrow-announces-new-Chief-Executive-Officer-8c2.aspx |archive-date=16 May 2014 }} The company agreed on 16 October 2014 to sell Glasgow, Southampton and Aberdeen airports to [[AGS Airports]], a consortium of [[Ferrovial]] and Macquarie Group for £1 billion, in order to focus solely on Heathrow.{{cite news|date=16 October 2014|title=Aberdeen, Glasgow and Southampton airports sold in £1bn deal|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-29650438|last=Fraser|first=Douglas|work=[[BBC News]]|location=[[Glasgow]]|publisher=[[BBC Scotland]]|access-date=20 October 2014|archive-date=19 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141019042448/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-29650438|url-status=live}}{{cite news|last=Calder|first=Simon|date=17 October 2014|title=What Glasgow, Aberdeen and Southampton airports sell-off means for passengers|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|location=Glasgow|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/news-and-advice/what-glasgow-aberdeen-and-southampton-airports-selloff-means-for-passengers-9802714.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220509/https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/news-and-advice/what-glasgow-aberdeen-and-southampton-airports-selloff-means-for-passengers-9802714.html |archive-date=9 May 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|access-date=20 October 2014}} === COVID-19 pandemic and new consortium === As of 2020, during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom|COVID-19 pandemic]] which enormously reduced air travel, the company had debts of over £17 billion to banks and bondholders. It is amongst the highest indebted UK companies, though 90% of its shares are held overseas. Its request in October 2020 to increase airport charges was rejected by the [[Civil Aviation Authority (United Kingdom)|Civil Aviation Authority]].{{cite news |last=Gill |first=Oliver |date=25 October |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230827165211/https://mediacentre.heathrow.com/pressrelease/detail/17082 |url-status=live }} ==Corporate affairs== [[File:BAA Limited logo.svg|thumb|The BAA logo, introduced in 1986]] As BAA, the company stated that its name did not stand for anything. It was still widely referred to as the "British Airports Authority" by both the media and the public, though the Authority was dissolved following the 1986 [[privatisation]].[https://web.archive.org/web/20080706025556/http://business.timesonline.co.uk/tol/business/industry_sectors/transport/article3792680.ece BAA plans clear-out of top managers] BAA should not be confused with BA, the abbreviation of [[British Airways]].The initials of the two companies were once used by a cartoonist in the ''[[Richmond and Twickenham Times]]'' accompanied by a parody of the familiar [[Baa, Baa, Black Sheep|nursery rhyme]]. The company's former logo, composed of three green triangles, was created by [[John Lloyd (graphic designer)|John Lloyd]] and Jim Northover of the design consultancy Lloyd Northover, at the time of the privatisation in 1986. The original BAA plc was acquired in 2006 by Airport Development and Investment Limited (ADI), a new company formed by the Ferrovial consortium. In October 2008, ADI changed its name to BAA Limited,[http://wck2.companieshouse.gov.uk//compdetails Companies House Webcheck] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081229053844/http://wck2.companieshouse.gov.uk/ |date=29 December 2008 }} Company number 05757208 and on 15 October 2012, the company announced that it had changed its name to Heathrow Airport Holdings. Colin Matthews, Chief Executive of the company, said that, given the reduction in the number of airports owned by the company, the BAA name was no longer appropriate; after the sale of Stansted, Heathrow Airport would account for 95% of the company's business. Each remaining airport owned by the company reverted to operating under its own name rather than the BAA banner.{{cite news |last=Thomas |first=Nathalie |date=15 October 2012 |title=BAA rebrands as 'Heathrow' |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/9610486/BAA-rebrands-as-Heathrow.html |newspaper=The Telegraph |access-date=20 October 2014 |archive-date=25 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925015022/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/9610486/BAA-rebrands-as-Heathrow.html |url-status=live }} As a major client of the UK construction industry, it is a member of the [[Construction Clients' Group]], which represents client views to the government's [[Strategic Forum for Construction]]. {| class="wikitable" |+Ownership (as FGP Topco Limited) |- ! "BAA plc 130 Wilton Road London SW1V 1LQ:" ===Flying matters=== BAA was a founding member of [[Flying Matters]],{{cite web|url=http://www.flyingmatters.co.uk/site/uk/about|publisher=Flying Matters|date=20 December 2007|title=Corporate website – about|access-date=23 December 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080123105729/http://www.flyingmatters.co.uk/site/uk/about |archive-date = 23 January 2008}} a coalition of business groups, trade unions, tourism groups and the aviation industry (airports, airlines, aerospace manufacturers and air traffic control){{cite web|url=http://www.flyingmatters.co.uk/templates/press_article.asp?PageID=27 |title=Voters in key marginals shun Conservative proposals for higher taxes on air travel |publisher=Flying Matters |access-date=7 July 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080316005615/http://www.flyingmatters.co.uk/templates/press_article.asp?PageID=27 |archive-date=16 March 2008}} The text of this source is the same color as the background; highlight it to read. launched in June 2007{{cite web |url=http://www.uk-airport-news.info/gatwick-airport-news-280507a.htm |title=Travel industry to launch climate-change lobby group : Gatwick Airport News Stories |publisher=Uk-airport-news.info |access-date=7 July 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090114080558/http://www.uk-airport-news.info/gatwick-airport-news-280507a.htm |archive-date=14 January 2009 }} to "balance the argument around issues of aviation and climate change" arguing that aviation does not contribute significantly to climate change, and that an expansion of aviation will aid the developing world, benefit social justice, and is essential for UK tourism and for the UK economy. The group was dissolved in April 2011 after several members, including BAA, left the coalition.{{cite web|url=http://www.travelweekly.co.uk/Articles/2011/04/11/36805/airline-industry-lobby-group-grounded-from-april.html|title=Airline industry lobby group grounded from April|work=Travel Weekly|access-date=20 October 2012|archive-date=14 April 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110414151226/http://www.travelweekly.co.uk/Articles/2011/04/11/36805/airline-industry-lobby-group-grounded-from-april.html|url-status=dead}} ===Expansion of Heathrow Airport=== {{main|Expansion of Heathrow Airport}} Since 2009 the company has been progressing a plan to build a third runway to expand Heathrow Airport. This requires government approval, and on 5 June 2018 [[Cabinet of the United Kingdom|the Cabinet]] approved the third runway, with a full vote planned for Parliament.{{cite web | title = Heathrow Airport: Cabinet approves new runway plan | url = https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-44357580 | date = 5 June 2018 | work = BBC News | access-date = 21 July 2018 | archive-date = 10 July 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180710095617/https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-44357580 | url-status = live }} The financing of the expansion has yet to be arranged, with Heathrow Airport Holdings' finances already highly [[Leverage (finance)|leveraged]]. In 2017 borrowings were £13.4 billion, with shareholders' equity at £0.7 billion.{{cite news |url=https://www.ft.com/content/98e6b128-7533-11e8-aa31-31da4279a601 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221210/https://www.ft.com/content/98e6b128-7533-11e8-aa31-31da4279a601 |archive-date=10 December 2022 |url-access=subscription |title=Who will pay for Sold in 2008 to [[Autogrill]]) ==Controversies== ===Heathrow management=== The company has received criticism for prioritising shops over extra security aisles at Heathrow. After much criticism for this, BAA removed some shops to provide extra security lanes. ''[[The Economist]]'' wrote that retail is important for BAA at Heathrow because, by law, landing charges are much less than those of similar-scope airports and shops help make up the difference. BAA has been accused of under-investing in snow and ice-fighting technology at Heathrow, which led to runway closures and severe delays in December 2010.{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-12049482|title=Has Heathrow's Reputation Been Damaged?|last=Musafer|first=Shanaz|work=BBC News|location=London|date=21 December 2010|archive-date=17 December 2018|access-date=20 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181217043915/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-12049482|url-status=live}}. In July 2019, Unite threatened a strike over pay after growing frustration on pay inequality. Whilst the CEO John Holland-Kaye was awarded a 103% pay rise from £2,100,000 to £4,200,000, staff have been denied a 4.5% increase.{{Cite news|url=https://www.itv.com/news/2019-07-12/heathrow-could-be-shut-down-this-summer-due-to-strike-action/|title=Heathrow Airport could be 'shut down' this summer owing to strike action|website=ITV News|location=London|publisher=ITN|date=12 July 2019|language=en|access-date=21 July 2019|archive-date=20 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190720190640/https://www.itv.com/news/2019-07-12/heathrow-could-be-shut-down-this-summer-due-to-strike-action/|url-status=live}} ===Heathrow protest injunction=== In July 2007, BAA sought an injunction preventing potential protesters involved in the [[Camp for Climate Action]] from approaching Heathrow Airport. The injunction specifically targeted anyone belonging to, or protesting in the name of, [[AirportWatch]], The No Third Runway Action Group and [[Plane Stupid]]. Airport Watch members included [[Friends of the Earth]], [[Greenpeace]], the [[Campaign to Protect Rural England]], the [[World Development Movement]], the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] and the [[Royal Society for the Protection of Birds]] – all of whom were caught by what was described as the 'Mother of all Injunctions'.{{cite web|url=http://www.newstatesman.com/200708130002 |title=The mother of all injunctions |publisher=New Statesman |date=13 August 2007 |access-date=7 July 2009}} BAA denied seeking a blanket ban on airport protest. In the end they won a more limited injunction,{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/6932519.stm |title=BAA wins Heathrow protesters ban |work=BBC News |date=6 August 2007 |access-date=7 July 2009 |archive-date=5 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170805184314/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/6932519.stm |url-status=live }} and the camp went ahead amid considerable worldwide publicity.{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/6943084.stm |title=Heathrow protesters set up camp |publisher=BBC News Online |date=12 August 2007 |access-date=7 July 2009 |archive-date=5 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170805184324/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/6943084.stm |url-status=live }} Afterwards, Duncan Bonfield, BAA director of corporate affairs, and Mark Mann, BAA head of media relations, resigned.{{cite news|url=http://uk.reuters.com/article/businessNews/idUKL2231571420070822 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080123225801/http://uk.reuters.com/article/businessNews/idUKL2231571420070822 |url-status=dead |archive-date=23 January 2008 |title=Two top press officers resign from BAA | Business |publisher=Uk.reuters.com |date=22 August 2007 |access-date=7 July 2009}} ===General aviation=== BAA's pricing structure mostly excludes [[General aviation in the United Kingdom|general aviation]] access to their airports by either banning the movements of light aircraft, or setting high fees and mandatory handling charges. The total charges for landing, one night of parking, and mandatory handling for a [[Cessna 152]] (including VAT) in 2013 was £234 at Aberdeen,[http://www.aberdeenairport.com/about-us/doing-business-with-us/conditions-of-use] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130603050043/http://www.aberdeenairport.com/about-us/doing-business-with-us/conditions-of-use |date=3 June 2013 }} BAA Aberdeen Conditions of Use £193 at Glasgow,[http://www.glasgowairport.com/about-us/doing-business-with-us/conditions-of-use] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130125010516/http://www.glasgowairport.com/about-us/doing-business-with-us/conditions-of-use|date=25 January 2013}} BAA Glasgow Conditions of Use and £187 at Southampton.[http://www.southamptonairport.com/about-us/doing-business-with-us/conditions-of-use] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120328045237/http://www.southamptonairport.com/about-us/doing-business-with-us/conditions-of-use|date=28 March 2012}} BAA Southampton Conditions of Use Heathrow Airport does not permit any flights for recreational, commemorative, charity and record breaking purposes, light twin-engine private aircraft and all light single-engine aircraft.[http://www.ead.eurocontrol.int/pamslight/pdf/4e415453/EG/C/EN/AIP/AD/EG_AD_2_EGLL_en] London Heathrow – AIP Textual Data BAA has since taken steps to improve this issue, including the waiving of mandatory handling fees for light aircraft at Aberdeen and Southampton. In 2014, the equivalent charges were £29.65 at Southampton and £64.63 at Aberdeen.{{Citation needed|date=August 2014}} However, the fees remained the same at Glasgow. It was also acknowledged that Heathrow Airport's runways are used at 99% of their capacity, and therefore the charges were set on the basis of very high demand and the lack of supply.{{cite web |url=http://www.acl-uk.org/reportsStatistics.aspx?id=98&subjectId=33 |title=Airport Coordination Limited - Reports/Statistics - Heathrow Airport |access-date=21 November 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129041412/http://www.acl-uk.org/reportsStatistics.aspx?id=98&subjectId=33 |archive-date=29 November 2014 }} ==See also== {{Portal|London|Companies|Aviation}} * [[List of companies based in London]] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== *{{official website}} {{authority control}} [[Category:Airport operators of the United Kingdom]] [[Category:Companies based in the London Borough of Hillingdon]] [[Category:Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec companies]] [[Category:Companies formerly listed on the Australian Securities Exchange]] [[Category:Companies formerly listed on the London Stock Exchange]] [[Category:Former cross-listed companies]] [[Category:Former nationalised industries of the United Kingdom]] [[Category:Heathrow Airport]] [[Category:Heathrow Airport Holdings| ]] [[Category:Public Investment Fund]] [[Category:Transport companies established in 1985]] [[Category:1985 establishments in England]]

Heathrow Airport Holdings is a company that operates and manages Heathrow Airport based in London, England. It was formed by the privatisation of the British Airports Authority as BAA plc as part of Margaret Thatcher's privatisation of government-owned assets, and was once a constituent of the FTSE 100 Index. 
BAA plc was bought in 2006 by a consortium led by Ferrovial, a Spanish firm specialising in the construction and operation of transport and urban infrastructure. In March 2009, the company was eventually required to sell Gatwick and Stansted airports; eventually BAA sold all its airports other than Heathrow and was renamed to its current name in 2012 to reflect its main business; businesses sold include the management of airports in the US and Africa, as well as the retailer World Duty Free. In 2024, Ferrovial sold most of its shares to the private capital Ardian and the Saudi Public Investment Fund, now among other foreign institutional investors. 
The company's head office is in the Compass Centre, on the grounds of Heathrow Airport in the London Borough of Hillingdon. The company makes money from charging landing fees and departing passenger levies to airlines, and from ancillary operations within those airports such as retail, car parking and property.
